paper_title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Most of the progress in language models over the past few years has been bought with scale. When model is not good enough, the standard answer is to make it bigger, and parameter counts are announced like trophies, as if size were the achievement. Bigger models are more capable, but they are also far more expensive to train and to serve, and the price of the most capable models keeps climbing even as the labs building them promise to bring it down. Too often the safe choice wins: another trillion parameters on recipe from 2023, rather than better recipe. Metis is Lernexs bet on the opposite direction. Better training data, better training algorithms and genuinely new architectures can buy capability that parameters alone cannot, and at fraction of the cost. single researcher cannot outspend frontier lab, but can out-iterate one: try an idea the day it occurs, build on the newest results instead of the safest ones, and take risks on designs large organization would not. Every part of the Metis stack is written from scratch, from data acquisition and decontamination to tokenization, training kernels, reinforcement-learning environments and evaluation, so any of it can change the moment better idea arrives. Metis-1.6 was never meant to beat frontier models. It was built to test that bet at small scale, and to answer more personal question: can I, starting from nothing, build each model better than the last, learn from every mistake, and get measurably better at the craft? Each Metis release is one step of that answer. Metis-1.5 was the first Metis model you could really talk to. Metis-1.6 is the first one you can realistically use: it works through olympiad problems, calls tools and follows instructions well enough to be genuinely helpful in places. Metis-1.7 comes next, and this report is, in large part, the story of how got ready to build it. Four generations of Metis were trained in 2026: Metis-1.3 (201M parameters): 28-layer dense hybrid of 21 Mamba-2 and 7 grouped-query attention blocks, with an 8,192-token vocabulary and 4,096-token context. Metis-1.4 (503.8M parameters): mixture-of-recursions transformer that explored weight-tied recurrent depth and taught me great deal about label-shift and residual-scaling instabilities in looped models. Metis-1.5 (897.4M total, 339.6M active parameters): 19-layer latent mixture-of-experts decoder (dmodel = 1,536, 32 routed experts with top-4 routing and one shared expert, 32,768token vocabulary), pretrained on 50B tokens and fine-tuned as Metis-1.5-think. Metis-1.6 Praxis and Logos: the two-pass looped hybrids of this report, pretrained on sixteen times the data of Metis-1.5, on AMD Instinct MI300A accelerators. This report has two jobs. The first is to measure the models honestly. Every comparison comes from one harness that ran Metis and every comparison model with identical prompts and scorers, and every comparison table is generated from the benchmark data published with the models. The second job is to write down what went wrong. Release reports usually describe the recipe that worked. This one also describes an optimizer that silently differed from its configuration for the entire pretraining run, component the model learned to switch off, and post-training choices that cost capability. would rather publish my mistakes than repeat them, and suspect they are the most useful pages here for anyone else building models without frontier budget. 3 Contributions. 1. Two open models with complete training lineage, checkpoint hashes and exact parameter accounting (Sections 3 to 8), evaluated with one harness against open models of similar size: 27 at the base stage and 28 after post-training (Section 9 and Appendices and B). 2. An audit of the pretraining optimizer. The declared AdaMuon optimizer was never instantiated, and because of parameter-routing mismatch every attention matrix trained with AdamW (Section 4.2). 3. negative result on hashed n-gram memory. In both models the learned injection gates closed, and deleting the 1.77B-parameter table from Logos changed held-out loss by less than 103 nats (Section 5). 4. Post-training lessons: five supervised fine-tuning failure modes; verifier imbalance that shortened reasoning on unseen science questions; and sign inversion of length rewards under group-mean normalization, proved and observed, with one-line fix (Sections 6 and 7). 5. Controlled 10B-token ablations of the loop design and optimizer behind MoRE, the architecture of Metis-1.7 (Section 10). Results in brief. Figure 1 is the picture would put on the fridge. Across 40 post-trained benchmarks, Logos averages 52.93: seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and 0.75 points behind Qwen3-4B. That is not frontier result, and the open models from large labs beat it more often than not. But Logos was trained on 1.02T tokens, against median of 12T for the comparators that disclose count, and every model above it that discloses its data was trained on at least 28T. It is also mixture-of-experts model running against mostly dense ones: it activates 2.36B parameters per token, while every model that beats it activates between 1.5 and 4.6 times as many. On both axes, Logos sits on the Pareto frontier, and in the shaded corner of each plot: higher score than the median model, on far less data and compute than it. Where it shines, it shines properly. In mathematics Logos ranks second of 30 models, behind only Gemma 4 12B, with the highest score in its set on HMMT February 2025 (62.92), HMMT February 2026 (63.64) and IMO-AnswerBench (57.00). Where it struggles, it struggles properly too: code, instruction following, long context and factual recall all trail models trained on small fraction of the data that the large labs use (Figure 3). Praxis averages 36.62 and, like Logos, sits on the compute frontier. As base models, both trail open models of similar size, which attribute mainly to training on one to two orders of magnitude fewer tokens (Appendix A). Availability. The four models, Metis-1.6-Logos, Metis-1.6-Praxis and their -Base counterparts, are published at https://huggingface.co/Lernex. All four ship without the n-gram memory (Section 5). sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Hybrid state-space models. Mamba-2 [12] recasts selective state-space models as structured attention and makes them efficient on matrix hardware. Hybrids that keep few attention layers among many state-space layers, such as Jamba [25] and Nemotron-H [29, 30], retain most of the quality of attention at fraction of the inference cost. Metis-1.6 places three attention layers among twenty (Logos) and two among twelve (Praxis), with no positional encoding. Looped and recurrent-depth models. Applying shared block repeatedly goes back to the Universal Transformer [14]. Recent work scales recurrent depth for latent reasoning [16], pretrains looped language models at scale [45], routes tokens to different recursion depths [6], and adds gated highways between loop iterations of mixture-of-experts models [17]. Metis-1.6 loops its entire stack fixed two times. Mixture-of-experts. Metis-1.6 follows fine-grained experts with shared expert [11], auxiliaryloss-free load balancing through routing biases [38] and router z-loss [46]. Experts operate in compressed latent space as in LatentMoE [15], with SwiGLU units [35]. Residual streams and memory. Hyper-connections [44] widen the residual stream into several streams with learned mixing. Manifold-constrained hyper-connections [13, 40] project the mixing matrix toward the doubly stochastic matrices with SinkhornKnopp iterations [37]. Conditional memory through hashed n-gram lookup [9] adds sparse parameter axis; Section 5 reports that the Metis models learned not to use it. 5 Optimizers. Muon [22, 27] orthogonalizes the momentum updates of matrix parameters with NewtonSchulz iterations. AdaMuon [36] and NorMuon [24] add second-moment normalization, and Polar Express [4] derives optimal polynomial iterations for the orthogonalization. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. GRPO [34] normalizes rewards within group of samples for the same prompt, and GSPO [42] moves importance ratios and clipping to the sequence level. Dr. GRPO [28] and DAPO [41] analyse and correct biases of the group objective. Length has been controlled with length penalties [5, 23] and length-conditioned training [2]. The sign inversion of Section 7.2 is direct consequence of mean-centring and is closely related to these analyses. On-policy distillation [1] trains student on its own samples against teachers distribution.

sections.title: 3 Architecture: one stack, two passes
sections.content: Praxis and Logos are the same architecture at two sizes (Figure 2 and Table 1). Instead of stacking more layers, Metis-1.6 runs its hybrid trunk twice for every token. Each token passes through 40 sequence-mixing and expert stages in Logos (20 layers, two passes) and 24 in Praxis (12 layers, two passes), while only half as many are stored. Parameter counts in this section are read directly from the tensor shapes of the released checkpoints. Hybrid trunk. Logos has 20 layers of width 2,560: grouped-query attention [3] at layers 5, 10 and 15, and Mamba-2 everywhere else. Praxis has 12 layers of width 2,048, with attention at layers 4 and 8. The Mamba-2 blocks use expansion 2 (dinner = 5,120 in Logos), state size 128, head dimension 64, width-4 causal convolution, chunk size 256, and 10 (Logos) or 8 (Praxis) B/C groups. Attention has head dimension 64, with 40 query and 10 key-value heads in Logos and 32 and 8 in Praxis, and uses no positional encoding at all. The Mamba-2 layers already know where each token sits, which is what lets the models stretch from 4,096 to 131,072 tokens without touching position handling (Section 4.3). It also means only 3 of Logoss 20 layers (2 of Praxiss 12) keep key-value cache, so memory grows slowly with context. To let attention behave differently on the second pass without storing second copy, each attention layer adds pass-indexed rank-8 low-rank update to its fused query-key-value projection. sections.title: 4.1 Data
sections.content: Both models were pretrained on the sealed metis-1.6-data-r2 release: 806 provenance-hashed shards totalling 804,755,808,835 tokens (SHA-256 65ef27f6...), served in three curriculum phases: 1. Phase (554,849,376,946 tokens, 68.9%): broad filtered web text, books, scientific articles and code. 2. Phase (209,668,641,449 tokens, 26.1%): up-weighted mathematics, science, software engineering and structured analytical text. 3. Phase (40,237,790,440 tokens, 5.0%): an annealing mix of curated technical prose, formal proofs, competition mathematics and reference documentation. Logos took 219,280 optimizer steps and ended at checkpoint ebddf9827d1a; Praxis took 191,870. Every shard was decontaminated against the evaluation benchmarks by 13-gram shingle matching. Each shard also carries sidecar (NGRAM_CANONICAL_IDS.uint16) that maps every token to canonical id, collapsing case, whitespace and punctuation variants, for the n-gram memory of Section 5.

sections.title: 4.2 The optimizer I thought I had
sections.content: The run configuration said optimizer.name: meant to carry over the AdaMuon implementation of Metis-1.5 [36], which keeps an elementwise second-moment buffer on the orthogonalized direction. Partway through the campaign audited the PyTorch trainer and the 100Badamuon. 8 and 600B-token Logos checkpoints, and found that the optimizer that actually ran was different animal in four ways, all present for the whole of pretraining: 1. The optimizer name was never read. The trainer always built Muon/AdamW hybrid with plain Muon and no second-moment state: Nesterov momentum 0.95; five Newton Schulz steps with coefficients (3.4445, 4.7750, 2.0315) in BF16; update RMS matched by 0.2pmax(r, c) scale; constant decoupled weight decay 0.1; and an unswept learning rate of 1.2 104 (Logos) or 1.8 104 (Praxis). 2. Attention trained with AdamW. The parameter router assigned Muon to attention matrices by matching names containing .mixer.impl., but the attention module was mounted directly at layers.N.mixer. Every attention projection, including the pass-specific low-rank updates, quietly fell through to the default group and trained with AdamW (β = (0.9, 0.95), ϵ = 108, weight decay 0.1) for all 804.76B tokens. 3. Fused projections were orthogonalized as one matrix. The Mamba-2 input projection (12,880 2,560 in Logos) concatenates five functionally different projections (z, x, B, and t). Muon orthogonalized it as single block, coupling singular vectors across gate, state and step-size projections. 4. Weight norms drifted apart. Between 100B and 600B tokens, weight RMS changed by factor of 0.88 to 0.91 for routed experts, 1.12 for Mamba input projections, 1.24 for Mamba output projections, 0.80 for shared-expert down projections, 0.57 for convolutions and 1.49 for the final norm. None of this stopped training, and the loss curve never said word. Every architectural conclusion in this report is therefore conditional on this optimizer. The lesson is cheap to apply: assert every parameters optimizer group at start-up. Section 10 measures what the corrected optimizer is worth.

sections.title: 4.3 Context extension
sections.content: From the 4,096-token checkpoints, both models continued pretraining on 18B tokens of long documents packed to at most 163,840 tokens. Logos took 1,968 optimizer steps (17,937,499,304 tokens) and Praxis 3,456 steps (18,000,000,000 tokens). Table 2 reports the extension gate on 384 held-out documents of 131,072 tokens, short-context retention on seven zero-shot tasks, and the 13-task RULER suite [20]. On Logos, top-1 retrieval of planted needle at 131,072 tokens rose from 19.53% to 68.75% at the 12B-token gate and 66.93% at 18B, while loss on the tail of full-length documents fell from 5.689 to 1.495 nats. RULER reached 84.48% at 4K, 73.25% at 32K and 60.14% at 128K, 1.32 points above the 12B-token gate at 128K, and the seven-task short-context mean barely moved (62.65 to 62.24). On Praxis, needle accuracy rose from 17.97% to 67.71% at the 6B-token gate, 66.15% at 12B and 65.63% at 18B; full-context tail loss fell from 5.735 to 1.614 nats and base-window loss from 1.703 to 1.665 nats. sections.title: 5 A memory the models chose to forget
sections.content: Following the Engram line of work [9], both models carried hashed n-gram conditional memory. For each position, the canonicalized preceding 2-grams and 3-grams are hashed into eight prime-modulus tables per order. In Logos the 2-gram tables have 1,723,303 to 1,730,101 rows and the 3-gram tables 1,730,507 to 1,737,161, each holding 64-dimensional values. The 16 retrieved vectors are concatenated, projected to model width, and the result mt is added to each residual stream at two layers of each pass (layers 2 and 5 in Logos, 2 and 4 in Praxis) through learned gate: g(ℓ,p) t,s = σ h(ℓ,p) t,s , v(ℓ,p) dmodel , + b(ℓ,p) t,s = h(ℓ,p) h(ℓ,p) t,s + g(ℓ,p) t,s mt. (2) The tables hold 1,774,549,800 parameters in Logos and 602,180,520 in Praxis, and were trained with sparse Adam at twice the base learning rate. The models had other plans. Both drove the gate biases negative and closed the gates  (Table 4)  . After pretraining, the mean gate at every injection site was between 0.0001 and 0.0031. After post-training it was at most 0.0141, and the memorys update to residual stream stayed below 0.85% of the streams norm everywhere. see two structural reasons: 1. Redundancy with early Mamba-2 convolutions. Layers 0 and 1 are Mamba-2 blocks whose width-4 causal convolutions already compute local 2-, 3and 4-gram compositions in continuous hidden space before the first injection at layer 2. 2. Hash-collision noise. With about 1.73M rows per table across 805B tokens, prime-modulus hashing aliases frequent and rare n-grams into the same rows. Injected into four residual streams that are refined over two passes, the noisy lookup costs more than it adds, and the gate bias receives steady gradient toward closing. So removing the memory is close to free. Deleting the 20 ngram_memory.* tensors moved bits per byte on pretraining prose from 0.733898 to 0.733894 on Logos and from 0.78110 to 0.78123 on Praxis. On 44,684 tokens of post-training text it changed the loss of released Logos by 0.000647 nats (1.184412 to 1.183764, 97.65% top-1 agreement), of Logos after reinforcement learning by +0.000112 nats (1.404278 to 1.404390, 96.70%), and of released Praxis by 0.001559 nats (1.281273 to 1.279714, 97.72%). For released Logos, the model is very slightly better without it. The released checkpoints ship without the memory: in BF16, Logos is 20.80 GB instead of 24.35 GB (model.safetensors SHA-256 965efc2f...), and Praxis 6.16 GB instead of 7.37 GB (SHA-256 861af5db...). sections.title: 6 Supervised fine-tuning, and five things I would do differently
sections.content: Both models were fine-tuned with response-only cross-entropy loss under the metis-chat/v1 template, which has two modes: in think mode the response opens with reasoning block, and in direct mode it answers straight away. Stage 1: cold-start fine-tuning used 120.01B tokens of long reasoning traces in mathematics, science and code. On Logos it took 8,182 steps and ended at 6958ef5907eb, with gates at 60B and 120B tokens. The 120B gate reached held-out response loss of 0.4612 (final training loss 0.2868) and, in think mode, 59.58% on pooled AIME, 50.82% on GPQA Diamond, 42.61% on HMMT February 2026 and 62.86% on MMLU. It was capable reasoner and poor assistant: 32.76% on IFEval and 12.40% on BFCL v4. Stage 2: overall fine-tuning used 80.00B tokens across every domain, including instruction following, tool calling and conversation. On Logos it took 2,735 steps and ended at 44b8e759242f, with gates at 40B (4538f48d884d) and 80B tokens. The 80B checkpoint kept the reasoning (60.00% on AIME, 52.02% on GPQA Diamond, 68.00% on MMLU and 56.14% on MMLU-Pro in think mode) and became an assistant: 71.07% on IFEval and 58.60% on BFCL v4. The reinforcement-learning stages of Section 7 traded breadth for shorter reasoning, so for both models released the end of Stage 2.

sections.title: 6.1 Five failure modes and their fixes in Metis-1.7
sections.content: 1. Direct-mode examples made by deletion. To build direct-mode examples, script (strip.py) deleted the reasoning block from 1525% of reasoning traces. Those traces define variables, helper functions and intermediate equations inside the reasoning block, so the remaining answer often refers to work the model never sees. That teaches direct mode to guess. At the cold-start gate, direct-mode IFEval trailed think mode by 10.92 points (21.84% against 32.76%). Fix: the deletion script is retired in favour of 12.0B tokens of direct-mode answers generated natively without reasoning and verified against ground-truth answers and unit tests. 2. Verification loops inherited from teachers. At the released Logos checkpoint, median think-mode lengths on the gate suite were 23,400 tokens on AIME (21.67% truncated at 64K), 42,377 on HMMT February 2026 (36.36% truncated) and 13,857 on GPQA Diamond. QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-R1-0528 traces in the fine-tuning pool recount or double-check four to seven times after the boxed answer is already derived, and Logos learned the habit faithfully. Fix: filter rejects traces with more than two post-solution verification passes, or more than 4,096 thinking tokens on prompts of difficulty at most 2/5, while keeping genuine 16K to 64K-token derivations in software engineering and olympiad mathematics. 3. hidden teacher mix. Of the 9.34M rows of openbmb/UltraData-SFT-2605, 6.93M (74.2%) came from early-2025 teachers: DeepSeek-R1-0528 (3.89M), Qwen2.5-72B (2.09M) and 12 QwQ-32B (740K). Fix: all 6.93M rows (about 18B tokens) are removed, and only late-2026 teachers are kept (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and GLM-5.3-Flash). 4. No voice of its own. Only 4,800 identity rows (0.008% of 60B tokens) and 15M tokens of open conversation (0.04% of 80B) entered training, and in open-ended chat Logos sounds like the average of its teachers. Fix: 2.5B tokens of writing in defined house voice (no trailing hook questions, sparing punctuation, no therapeutic clichés) and 600M epoch-weighted tokens of multi-turn identity data. 5. Off-policy cross-entropy in Stage 2. Token-level cross-entropy on teacher text applies unbounded log πθ(y <t) gradients to low-probability stylistic tokens, which collapses generation entropy before reinforcement learning even starts. Fix: Stage 2 moves to reference-anchored sampling objective, x, L(x, y) = clip 1 y t=1 !0.25 πθ(y πref(y x, <t) x, <t) log πθ(y , 0.2, 2.5 x, <t), (3) mixed with 10% standard cross-entropy. The reference log-probabilities are precomputed offline in FP16, so the reference model costs no accelerator memory during training.

sections.title: 7 Reinforcement learning on Logos
sections.content: Starting from the released Logos checkpoint, ran six-stage reinforcement-learning and distillation study: hybrid-mode GSPO [42], five domain specialists, and on-policy distillation of the specialists back into one model. None of it became the released model. All of it taught me something. Table 5 gives the eight-suite gate for every checkpoint.

sections.title: 7.1 Teaching brevity with the wrong curriculum
sections.content: hybrid_mode_gspo ran for 264 optimizer steps over 79 rounds and ended at ea50ea259f48. It sampled 16 responses per prompt and alternated two short rounds at short response cap with one long round at the full cap. Systems. Three changes kept rollout generation from eating the run: 1. Fused decode kernels. fused routing statistics and ragged expert dispatch, injected depth memory without copies and precomputed dispatch constants, taking each decode step from about 8,000 small kernel launches to one compact captured graph. 2. Two-cohort cap ratcheting. The response cap tightened by 4,096 tokens whenever two consecutive closed cohorts had less than 1% truncation among correct samples and less than 2% among hard correct ones. It stepped from 49,152 to 20,480 tokens (Appendix D) and was inherited by every downstream specialist. 3. Memory. The rollout cache is released before the packed backward pass, and device-memory guard is anchored at 100.01 GiB (26 GB reserve). Peak reserved memory stayed at 74.60 GiB in GSPO and 60.57 to 66.38 GiB in the specialists, with no out-of-memory failures. Verifier imbalance. At step 198 (75e8704e) the gate suite told two stories at once. Think-mode IFEval had jumped 13.41 points, from 71.07% to 84.48% at median of 243 tokens, and direct-mode GPQA Diamond had risen from 32.83% to 35.35%. Meanwhile think-mode GPQA Diamond had fallen from 52.02% to 43.43% (median 2,687 tokens, 5.2 times shorter), and pooled AIME from 60.00% to 40.00% (3,713 tokens, 6.3 times shorter). The prompt pool explains it: 75.3% of prompts were formatting and tool-calling tasks: 48.3% function calls, 19.1% instruction constraints and 7.8% JSON schemas; 24.7% were mathematics with numeric answers; none were science, because all 15,235 science problems of PrimeIntellect/INTELLECT-3-RL had been set aside for the reasoning specialist. Three quarters of the reward came from tasks that 150to 400-token checklist solves. Rewarding brevity there taught the policy to answer graduate-level science with checklist too. Fix: in Metis-1.7 this stage becomes 48to 64-step domain-balanced bridge (30% mathematics, 20% science and STEM multiple choice, 15% code with unit tests, 15% instruction following, 10% tool calls, 10% knowledge questions), so science verifiers guard reasoning depth while length falls.

sections.title: 7.2 Punished for being right
sections.content: The specialists used gated length reward with λ = 0.5. Within prompt group that passes the gate, correct sample receives reward 1 if its length is at most the median length of the groups correct samples, and 1 λ if longer; an incorrect sample receives 0. Advantages are group-mean centred, Ai = (ri r)/σ, with σ > 0 batch-level scale. That sounds harmless. It is not. Proposition 1. Consider group of samples of which fraction is correct. Let fraction of the correct samples be short (reward 1) and 1 long (reward 1 λ, 0 < λ < 1). Then every long correct sample has negative advantage if and only if > 1 λ 1 λ(1 q) . With the median split (q = 1/2) and λ = 1/2, the threshold is > 2/3, that is, at least 11 correct samples out of 16. Proof. The group mean is = [ + (1 q)(1 λ) ] = [1 λ(1 q)]. long correct sample has = (1 λ r)/σ, which is negative exactly when 1 λ < [1 λ(1 q)]. In words: once prompt becomes easy, the policy gradient lowers the probability of every correct solution longer than the group median, however valid its reasoning. The reward punishes the model for showing its work. The reasoning specialist, trained on mathematics and science verifiers (INTELLECT-3-RL mathematics and science, UltraData-RL-2609 mathematics), followed the script almost exactly: Step 40 (389c7007). The first 40 steps won back what late GSPO had lost. Think-mode GPQA Diamond rose 8.08 points, from 35.86% to 43.94%, at median of 1,122 tokens, 12.3 times shorter than the released model. The rest of GPQA Main reached 38.40%, 2.80 points above the released model at 16.2 times fewer tokens. MMLU-Pro reached 57.29% at 843 tokens, against the released models 56.14% at 5,590. HMMT February 2026 tripled, from 12.12% to 36.36%. 14 Step 50 (9c708434). HMMT February 2026 rose to 42.42%, 3.03 points above the released model at median of 7,964 tokens against 42,377. Pooled AIME reached 35.00%, direct-mode IFEval 84.29% and direct-mode MMLU-Pro 47.29%. Step 78 (c640b106). The mean group pass rate had crossed 56.7%, and high-pass groups now exceeded > 2/3. With the length budget at 1,240 tokens, the inversion pushed down every correct derivation longer than that. GPQA Diamond fell back to 34.34% (median 676 tokens) and HMMT February 2026 to 24.24%. Step 40 is the tell. Short reasoning was never the problem: the decline came from negative advantages on valid 1,200to 3,000-token derivations, not from the response cap. The fix is one line. Clamp the advantage of correct samples at zero, Ai max(0, Ai) for every correct sample i, (4) which keeps the positive signal for short correct samples, removes the negative one for long correct samples, and still pushes down incorrect ones. The code, knowledge and agentic specialists trained with the clamp. The knowledge specialist raised HMMT February 2026 by 21.21 points over the GSPO checkpoint, to 33.33%, and reached 84.10% on direct-mode IFEval. The reasoning specialist had already finished before the clamp existed and was not rerun with it.

sections.title: 7.3 Agents waiting on containers
sections.content: The first rounds of the agentic specialist took more than 15 minutes each, for three reasons: 1. sandbox containers for all 64 episodes were started one by one before rollout began, although 95% of prompts were single-call tool-schema checks that never needed sandbox at all; 2. episodes cancelled when round reached its target never released their filesystem mounts; 3. records cancelled in short rounds were deferred to later rounds, which forced full, uncancelled long rounds every third round. Starting sandbox only at an episodes first tool call, closing every episode environment in finally block, and retiring cancelled records instead of deferring them fixed all three. Round times fell to those in Table 17, the deferral queue stayed empty, and the cap ratcheted four times, from 20,480 to 4,096 tokens, with no truncation. Among post-GSPO checkpoints, the agentic specialist set the highest scores on BFCL v4 in think mode (52.80%) and direct mode (47.20%), IFEval in think mode (84.10%), GPQA Diamond in direct mode (38.89%) and MMLU in think mode (67.14%).

It did not capture the peaks of the step-40 reasoning or agentic specialists, and for three unglamorous reasons: 1. One step, at warm-up speed. 224 trajectories on 224 data-parallel ranks with no gradient accumulation made exactly one optimizer step. sections.title: 9.3 Base models
sections.content: As base models, both Metis models trail most open models of similar size (Appendix A). Over the 44 short-context benchmarks, the Logos base averages 31.03, ahead only of OLMoE-1B-7B (29.44) in its set, and the Praxis base averages 24.66, last in its set. sections.title: 11 Limitations
sections.content: Recent contests. The decontamination manifest predates several of the contests reported here: AIME 2025 and 2026, HMMT 2025 and 2026, Brumo 2025, IMO-AnswerBench and Apex 2025 are 22 not on it. Logos is strongest relative to its comparators on exactly these benchmarks, so dedicated overlap check against them is the first thing will add. Harness. All comparisons use the Lernex harness, prompts and scorers. Comparators may do better under their developers recommended settings. Confounded architecture conclusions. Metis-1.6 trained attention with AdamW and everything else with plain Muon (Section 4.2), so its results do not isolate the architecture. The 10B-token ablations use corrected optimizer, but on smaller proxy with one run per arm, so their standard errors reflect evaluation noise rather than run-to-run variance. Reinforcement learning. The advantage clamp was used in the code, knowledge and agentic specialists, which were short runs, and not in the reasoning specialist where the sign inversion was observed.

sections.title: 12 Conclusion: talk, use, and what comes next
sections.content: Metis-1.5 was the first Metis model you could talk to. Metis-1.6 is the first you can use. Built end to end by one researcher on 1.02T tokens, Logos finishes ahead of open models trained on up to 38T tokens and within point of one trained on 36T, sits on the Pareto frontier for both data and compute, and on contest mathematics stands next to the best small models from the large labs. It is not frontier model, it does not pretend to be, and it still loses most head-to-head comparisons outside mathematics. It was never meant to win them. It was meant to prove can build, learn and build better, and the record says can. It is also the first real evidence for the bet Metis is built on: that the cheaper path to capable model runs through better data, algorithms and architectures, not more parameters. That record is the other half of this report: an optimizer that differed from its configuration for an entire run; memory the models chose not to use; fine-tuning data that taught habits did not want; length reward that, under group normalization, punished correct reasoning; distillation step too small to move the weights. Every one of them has been diagnosed, and every one has already changed how Metis-1.7 and MoRE are built. That is the part of this work am proudest of. Not any single score, but the loop behind it: build model, measure it honestly, find exactly where was wrong, and carry the lesson into the next one. Metis-1.3 taught me to train hybrid. Metis-1.4 taught me what breaks in looped model. Metis-1.5 learned to hold conversation, and Metis-1.6 learned to be useful. Each one did something the one before it could not. am not going to make promises about Metis-1.7 in these pages. would rather show you. What can say is that have never been more excited to share what comes next, and that intend to keep working the way this report does: in the open, learning fast, publishing the mistakes alongside the results, and, hope, surprising few people along the way. Metis started as bet that better idea can do what bigger budget cannot. Every release so far has made that bet look little better. See you at Metis-1.7.
